section: D.4 Choose a chart that matches the question
text:
D.4 Choose a chart that matches the question



Question
Common starting chart




How often does each category appear?
Bar chart


How is one numeric variable distributed?
Histogram or box plot


Which categories have larger values?
Ordered bar chart or dot plot


How do distributions differ across groups?
Box plot


Are two numeric variables related?
Scatterplot


How did a value change over time?
Line chart


Does geographic pattern matter?
Map supported by a table



The chart title should name the measure actually calculated. Avoid a line between observations that do not have a meaningful order.

title: Appendix D — Final Project
text:
D.5 Save a chart

ggsave("outputs/main-chart.png", main_chart)

ggsave() has optional arguments for width, height, and resolution when a publishing platform has specific requirements. Begin with the filename and chart object, then add those options only if they are needed.

title: Appendix D — Final Project
section: D.6 Make an evidence table before drafting
text:
D.6 Make an evidence table before drafting
An evidence table connects possible claims to calculations and reporting still needed. Fill it with actual values and source checks rather than drafting from memory or from the appearance of a chart:








Possible claim
Evidence in the data
What still needs checking?




One category has the largest total
Group summary and source row
Confirm the value and unit


One group has the largest share
Numerator and full denominator
Check excluded or missing categories


A measure increased over time
Comparable annual observations
Investigate changes in definitions


Two variables appear related
Table and scatterplot
Find evidence that could explain the pattern



The table can confirm, narrow, or reject the original story hypothesis.

title: Appendix D — Final Project
text:
D.7 Separate description from explanation
A dataset can identify and measure a pattern without explaining why it occurred. Explanations may require documents, interviews, subject expertise, or another dataset.






A pattern is not an explanation



Use the data to describe what changed, differed, or appeared related. Treat a possible explanation as a reporting lead until additional evidence supports it. A plausible explanation does not become a fact because it fits the chart.

title: Appendix D — Final Project
Appendix D — Final Project
section: D.9 Write a short methods note

title: Appendix D — Final Project
text:
D.10 Organize the story
A concise data story can follow this order:

Lead: the strongest verified finding.
Context: what the data cover and why the finding matters.
Evidence: a clear table or chart with exact values.
Reporting: documents or interviews that test explanations.
Limitations: what the evidence cannot show.
Methods: source, period, unit of analysis, and main calculation.

The goal is not to include every calculation. Select the evidence that answers the reporting question and helps the reader understand why it matters.

title: Appendix D — Final Project
section: D.11 Prepare the final project proposal

title: Appendix D — Final Project
text:
D.12 Final project checklist

The question is focused enough to answer with the available data.
The original data are preserved unchanged.
The source, access date, and reporting period are recorded.
The meaning of one row is stated.
Important filters and exclusions are explained.
Every percentage has a clear denominator.
Join keys and unmatched rows are checked.
The main numbers agree with the source or a second calculation.
Every major possible claim appears in the evidence table.
Chart titles, labels, units, and sources are complete.
Explanations and causal language have evidence beyond a visible pattern.
Relevant documents, experts, or interviews have been used to test explanations.
The limitations are written for the reader.
The R Markdown document knits after restarting R.

E.2 Lab A: Hong Kong graduate salary averages
The source columns are long, so rename them after importing:

library(tidyverse)

salary <- read_csv("data/hksalary.csv") |>
  rename(
    academic_year = `Academic Year`,
    level = `Level of Study`,
    programme = `Broad Academic Programme Category`,
    average_salary = `Average Annual Salary (HK$'000)`
  )

glimpse(salary)

Rows: 368
Columns: 4
$ academic_year  <chr> "2009/10", "2009/10", "2009/10", "2009/10", "2009/10", …
$ level          <chr> "Sub-degree", "Sub-degree", "Sub-degree", "Sub-degree",…
$ programme      <chr> "Medicine, Dentistry and Health", "Sciences", "Engineer…
$ average_salary <dbl> 292, 125, 125, 139, 163, 122, 155, 346, 148, 154, 157, …



Understand the rows
One row represents a published average salary for one academic year, study level, and broad programme category. The file does not contain individual graduates or the number of graduates behind each average.
This means that averaging all rows would create an unweighted mean of published programme averages. It would not be the average salary of all graduates.


Tasks

Count the rows for each academic year.
Choose one study level.
Compare the same programme categories over time.
Find the five largest published programme averages in the latest year.
Create one line or bar chart with an exact measure in the title.
List the additional data needed to calculate an overall graduate-weighted average.



Reporting check
Write a headline that refers to published programme-level averages, not “the average Hong Kong graduate.”

E.5 Takeaways







Function or practice
Why it matters




rename()
Makes long source column names easier to use


pivot_longer()
Turns many year columns into a tidy year variable


parse_integer()
Converts year text into whole numbers


Fixed comparison set
Keeps the same places or programmes in each period


Source check
Confirms that a surprising result is not an import or coding error









Want more control?



The official tidyr reference explains additional reshaping controls. The essential pivot_longer() arguments shown in this lab are enough for the supplied file.
